source.title: MLLMs Fail to Refuse when Using Tools Agentically
source.authors: Rikiya Takehi; Ryo Hachiuma; Shaona Ghosh; Dan Zhao; Yu-Chiang Frank Wang; Yusuke Hirota

page_placements.theme: Chat refusal does not guarantee safe agent or tool actions

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful-request refusal in a new setting—agentic multimodal tool use—rather than testing the fine-tuning, token-position, prefix, suffix, decoding, or parameter-localization claims in V1–V7.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures harmful-request refusal failure with and without tool use. Tool-use results are recorded under fits_no_version because tool use is not one of the interventions named by V1–V7, and the paper does not test the first-token mechanism. It also reports prompt, tool-output, reinjection, and answer-opening analyses; these are recorded where they report outcomes. Cited prior findings are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-request refusal failure when agentic tool use (ReAct with zoom, OCR, tagging and code) is enabled versus disabled in multimodal LLMs. None of V1–V7's interventions or measures appear. There is no fine-tuning, no per-token KL against a base model, no prefilling, suffix or decoding attack, no parameter localization, and no deepening training. The answer-opening analysis (Fig. 5) covers only successfully refused samples, so it is not a compliance rate for a bypassed opening. Qi et al. 2025 [45] is cited only to justify looking at how responses begin. The reader's 'tests/T3' is wrong: tool use is not a version's setting, so the study bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also argue that no-tool safety alignment should not be assumed to transfer to agentic settings. They recommend evaluating and training models under tool-using conditions.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates adding agentic tool use to MLLMs; does not reproduce the original fine-tuning interventions or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with tool availability and benchmark/model. More tool calls are associated with higher refusal failure; reinjecting the original request and image reduces it. The tool-output ablation reports similar RFR for standard and fake zoom. Prompt structure has a smaller reported effect than tool availability.

fits_no_version.finding: Enabling ReAct tool use raises refusal failure on every model × benchmark pair (Table 1; McNemar p<0.05 in Table 5). The native Gemini-3-Flash Agentic Vision system shows the same rise (+15.2 average).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Enabling agentic tool use increases multimodal models' failure to refuse harmful user requests relative to the same model without tools.

fits_no_version.finding: The tool-use effect persists under minimal prompts (+3.8±0.4) versus structured prompts (+4.2±0.5). Prompt structure alone shifts refusal failure by at most +0.5±0.4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tool-use refusal degradation is not an artifact of prompt format.

fits_no_version.finding: Reinjecting the original request and image before the final answer lowers refusal failure by 7.6% on average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Restoring the salience of the harmful request partially mitigates tool-use refusal failures.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal failure rises with the number of tool calls among items the no-tool model refused. Fake zoom returning the original image gives similar refusal failure to real zoom (34.2 vs 34.0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trajectory length, not tool-output content, is associated with tool-use refusal failure.

fits_no_version.finding: Among items refused in both settings, tool-use answers more often open with observation summaries (52.3%) and less often with direct refusals (55.6%→37.4%) or safety statements (25.8%→10.3%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tool use shifts the opening focus of refusals away from safety toward visual observation.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: The safety judgement primarily relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-5.2), although the paper reports 97% agreement with human ratings on 100 sampled responses. The authors note that utility-safety tradeoffs were out of scope. Some analyses are presented in figures without numerical values stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports further per-model/per-dataset McNemar-test results in Table 5, fuller per-model tool-call plots in Figure 8, and qualitative examples in Figures 4, 6, and 9–11; these were not separately extracted because of the 60-row limit and because they duplicate or illustrate the recorded outcomes. Figure 3’s individual model values and Figure 7’s individual-model values were not stated numerically in the text.

untested.parts: No aligned-vs-base per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling of a compliant start, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. The tool-trajectory content inserted before the answer is not a compliant prefix.
No localization of safety to weights or ranks.
No test of data or objective as the cause of shallowness.
No deepening training. Request reinjection is an inference-time mitigation for tool-use degradation, not deep alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T3' relation is corrected to cites_only/T6. The only link to the shallow-alignment literature is citing Qi et al. 2025 to motivate the answer-opening analysis. Conceptually, the context-dilution finding resembles 'safety decided early and easily displaced', but the study does not frame or test it as such. Safety judgments come from a single GPT-5.2 judge with 97/100 human agreement.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful examples or measure the effect of a few to a few hundred such examples.
Does not fine-tune on benign data or measure harmful compliance after benign fine-tuning.
Does not compare aligned and base models using per-token KL divergence or measure its distribution over response positions.
Does not test compliant-prefix prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal.
Does not localize safety behaviour to weights, parameters, or ranks.
Does not test whether training data or training objectives produce safety shallowness.
Does not train safety to extend beyond initial response tokens or evaluate whether such training holds up.

relation.reason: Section 4.2 includes the original shallow-alignment paper [45] in a grouped citation motivating response-opening analysis, without testing its token-level finding.

tranche.reason: Tool availability and prompt-format comparisons test refusal degradation, without testing or operationally using any V1–V7 claim.

source_check.notes: The numerical rows and synthesis statement match Table 2. These are auxiliary tool-use findings outside V1–V7; their behavioral descriptions should not be interpreted as claim-version states.
